content.text: This page presents the main graphs and metrics of the LTE network simulation model. They allow visualizing scheduler performance, evaluating resource allocation, and analyzing user behavior.

content.title: Metrics and Graphs
items: Cell Throughput: the total number of bits transmitted by all users per unit of time.
User Throughput: the number of bits transmitted to an individual user over a time interval.
Jain's Fairness Index: shows the evenness of resource distribution among users (1 — full fairness).
Spectral Efficiency: the efficiency of frequency spectrum usage, measured in bits/s/Hz.
User Mobility Map: visualizes user trajectories and analyzes the impact of mobility on connection quality.
CQI and Channel Conditions: shows channel quality (CQI) and SINR changes for each user.
Traffic Generation: user activity according to Full Buffer, Bursty Traffic, ON/OFF, and MMPP scenarios.
Resource Block Allocation (Resource Grid): shows RB allocation to each user in every TTI for RR, PF, and Best CQI schedulers.
ML Scheduler Results: visualization of machine learning algorithms (e.g., CatBoost) and comparison with baseline schedulers.

content.title: 1. Global Simulation Parameters
content.text: These parameters define the overall course of the simulation: when it starts, how long it lasts, how often data is updated, and how many users participate.
items: Simulation Duration (ms) – total duration of the simulation in milliseconds.
Num Frames – number of frames for the simulation.
Update Interval (ms) – interval for data updates in milliseconds.
Num Users – number of users in the simulation.
content.note: Key point: these parameters control the simulation timeframe and scale but do not define the behavior of individual objects.

content.title: 2. Configurable Model Parameters
content.text: These parameters define the behavior of individual objects within the simulation. They allow the user to flexibly configure each network component: users, base stations, channels, traffic, and schedulers. Using these settings, different LTE network scenarios can be modeled, including user density, environmental characteristics, and load types.

content.title: 2.1. Mobility Models
content.text: These models describe how and where users move during the simulation. The choice of model affects the spatial distribution of users and network load dynamics.
items: RandomWalkModel — the user moves randomly within defined area boundaries (x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max). Suitable for basic testing.
RandomWaypointModel — the user selects a random destination, moves to it, pauses (pause_time), and repeats the process.
GaussMarkovModel — ensures smooth and predictable user movement, controlling parameters α (memory coefficient) and boundary_threshold (boundary limit).
content.note: User movement directly affects channel quality, handover frequency between base stations, and scheduler efficiency.

content.title: 2.2. Channel Models
content.text: These models describe signal transmission characteristics between the base station and users, considering obstacles and environmental conditions.
items: RMaModel, UMaModel, UMiModel — different urban or rural scenarios, considering distance, building height, street width, and other factors.
Model parameters: bs — base station object, height, width — building dimensions, cond_update_period — channel state update frequency.
content.note: A correct channel model helps evaluate real-world conditions and adapt schedulers to changing circumstances.

content.title: 2.3. Traffic Models
content.text: These models define how data is generated by users, simulating various load scenarios.
items: PoissonModel — packets are generated at a specific rate (packet_rate) with fixed or random sizes.
OnOffModel — the user alternates between ON and OFF states, transmitting data only in the active phase; state durations and packet frequency are specified.
content.note: Different traffic types allow testing schedulers under stable and variable loads, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses.

content.title: 2.4. Base Station (BS Module)
content.text: Base station parameters describe its physical location and technical characteristics.
items: x, y — base station coordinates
height — antenna height
frequency_GHz — operating frequency
bandwidth — channel bandwidth
global_max, per_ue_max — buffer and resource limits
content.note: Station position and parameters affect coverage, signal strength, and resource allocation among users.

content.title: 2.5. User Equipment (UE Module)
content.text: These parameters define the characteristics of each user device.
items: UE_ID — unique user identifier
x, y — initial coordinates
buffer_size — buffer size for data storage
ue_class — user type (e.g., pedestrian)
content.note: Device differences allow modeling diverse network usage scenarios.

content.title: 2.6. Scheduler
content.text: The scheduler defines the resource allocation strategy among users.
items: Round Robin — equal distribution of resources
Proportional Fair — balance between efficiency and fairness
Max C/I — prioritizes users with the best channel quality
content.note: The choice of scheduler directly affects throughput, service quality, and fairness in resource allocation.

content.title: 1. Scenario Selection (Optional)
content.text: The user can choose a demonstration scenario for a quick introduction to the simulator. This step is optional — you can proceed directly to parameter configuration.
items: For beginners: click the «Overview» button on the home page to launch a demonstration scenario with preloaded settings.
For experienced users: you can skip this step and go straight to configuring simulation parameters.
content.note: Selecting a scenario allows for quick testing of the simulation but does not affect the ability to configure parameters individually.

content.title: 2. Enter Parameters
content.text: The user configures simulation and model parameters, including UE, BS, channel, traffic, and scheduler.
items: User Equipment parameters (number, identifiers, UE class).
Mobility models (RandomWalk, RandomWaypoint, Gauss-Markov).
Base Station parameters (coordinates, antenna height, frequency, channel bandwidth).
Channel parameters (select model: RMa, UMa, UMi).
Traffic parameters (Poisson, On/Off, MMPP) and intensity.
Resource scheduler selection (Round Robin, Proportional Fair, Max C/I).
content.note: All parameters can be changed before starting the simulation or during runtime for experiments with dynamic scenarios.

content.title: 3. JSON Upload
content.text: If the user wants to use a previously saved configuration, a JSON file with settings can be uploaded.
items: Open the «Load Configuration» modal window.
Select a file from your computer or enter a JSON link.
Click «Load» to apply the settings to the simulation.
content.note: Uploading JSON allows quickly restoring complex settings without manual input.

content.title: 4. Launch Simulation
content.text: After configuring parameters and (optionally) selecting a scenario, you can launch the simulation.
items: Click the «Start Simulation» button on the «Settings» tab.
Monitor the process in the «Graphs» tab, where charts and metrics are displayed.
Use the «Pause» or «Clear Parameters» buttons as needed to control the simulation.
content.note: After the simulation is complete, you can save the configuration and results for further analysis.

content.title: 1. Multi-Chart Synchronization
content.text: Multiple charts can be displayed simultaneously to compare different metrics or users. Synchronization ensures consistent time axes across charts.
items: Scrolling one chart horizontally updates the time axis on all synchronized charts.
Zooming or scaling one chart is reflected on all synchronized charts to maintain comparison context.
content.note: Synchronized charts make it easier to analyze correlations between metrics, such as user throughput and resource allocation.

content.title: 2. Interaction Between Visualizations
content.text: Charts and maps are interactive, allowing users to focus on specific data points or users.
items: Selecting a user on the User Movement Map highlights their data on all related charts.
Hovering over a metric on a chart displays additional details, such as exact values, timestamps, and related events.
Users can toggle chart visibility, choose which metrics to display, and compare multiple users or base stations simultaneously.
content.note: Interactive visualizations help in diagnosing issues, understanding performance patterns, and comparing different simulation scenarios.

content.title: 1. Saving Configurations
content.text: Users can save the current simulation settings to a JSON file for later use or sharing.
items: Open the 'Save Configuration' modal window.
Enter a file name in the 'Enter configuration name' field.
Add a description in the 'Description' field for easier identification.
Click 'Save' to create a JSON file with the current simulation settings.
content.note: Saving configurations allows you to quickly restore settings without manual input.

content.title: 2. Loading Configurations
content.text: To use a previously saved configuration, you can load a JSON file.
items: Open the 'Load Configuration' modal window.
Select a file from your computer or enter a link to a JSON file.
Click 'Load' to apply the settings to the simulation.
content.note: Loading a JSON file allows you to quickly restore complex configurations and reuse them for repeated experiments.

content.title: 3. File Naming Recommendations
items: Use clear names that include a description of the scenario (e.g., "high_load_scenario.json").
Add a date or version to distinguish updated configurations (e.g., "v1_2025-12-23.json").
Avoid spaces and special characters in file names.

content.title: 4. Configuration Versioning
content.text: To manage settings effectively, it is recommended to maintain versioned configurations when making changes.
items: Create a new file version with a changed name whenever significant parameters are modified.
Use version descriptions to explain which parameters were changed.
Keep all versions to allow rollback to previous settings.
content.note: Versioning helps track experiments, compare results, and prevent loss of important settings.

content.title: 5. JSON Usage Examples
items: Scenario for testing maximum load: "max_load_test_v1.json".
Scenario with varied UE models: "mobility_varied_v2.json".
Scenario for ML scheduler analysis: "ml_scheduler_comparison_v1.json".
content.note: Examples help users quickly navigate and create their configurations in a clear structure.

userDevice.title: User Equipment (UE) parameters. Used to define the number of devices and their identifiers participating in the network simulation.

DopUserDevice.title:
User Equipment (UE_MODULE).

Allows creating and configuring each UE individually. In the future, the model will be extended to support UE collections.

UE parameters:
UE_ID — unique user identifier.
x — initial X coordinate (m), default 0.0.
y — initial Y coordinate (m), default 0.0.
buffer_size — buffer size (bytes), default 1048576.
ue_class — user class (indoor, pedestrian, cyclist, car), default: pedestrian.

mobility.title:
User Equipment mobility models (MOBILITY_MODEL).

Random Walk Model — random movement within a defined area.
Random Waypoint Model — movement between random points with pauses.
Random Direction Model — movement in a random direction with pauses.
Gauss Markov Model — movement with memory of the previous state.

Parameters used:
x_min, x_max — X-axis boundaries (m)
y_min, y_max — Y-axis boundaries (m)
pause_time — pause between movements (ms, only for waypoint/direction models)

traffic.title:
Traffic models (TRAFFIC_MODEL).

PoissonModel — packet flow with a fixed average arrival rate.
OnOffModel — alternating active and inactive transmission phases.
MMPPModel — Markov Modulated Poisson Process (under development).

Parameters:
packet_rate — traffic intensity (packets/sec)
duration_on — duration of active phase (sec)
duration_off — duration of inactive phase (sec)

scheduler.title:
Resource scheduler (SCHEDULER).

RoundRobin — evenly distributes resources among users.
BestCQI — selects the user with the best channel quality.
ProportionalFair — balances throughput and fairness.

enodeb.title:
Base Station (BS_MODULE).

Allows creating and configuring a base station. The user can define its location and radio parameters.

Parameters:
x — X coordinate of the station (m), default 0.0.
y — Y coordinate of the station (m), default 0.0.
height — antenna installation height (m), default 35.0.
frequency_GHz — operating frequency (GHz), default 1.8.
bandwidth — channel bandwidth (MHz), default 10.

channel.title:
Channel Models (CHANNEL_MODEL)

The channel model describes radio signal propagation conditions between the base station and the UE. Different models correspond to different types of urban environments.

RMaModel (Rural Macro)
Used for rural areas and open spaces with low building density.
Characterized by long distances and minimal obstacles.
Parameters:
W — average street width (m), default 20.0
h — average building height (m), default 5.0
cond_update_period — channel update period (ms), default 0.0

UMaModel (Urban Macro)
Used for dense urban environments with tall buildings and long-range links between UE and BS.
Parameters:
cond_update_period — channel update period (ms), default 0.0
o2i_model — indoor penetration model ('low' | 'high'), default 'low'

UMiModel (Urban Micro)
Used for urban environments with short distances between devices and the base station.
Parameters:
cond_update_period — channel update period (ms), default 0.0
o2i_model — indoor penetration model ('low' | 'high'), default 'low'
